claim: Human loss aversion is real on average but its size depends on design: raw meta-analytic lambda is about 1.96 (Brown 2024, 93.9% of estimates above 1), but only 1.07 in symmetric unordered designs (Yechiam & Zeif 2025) and 1.31 in Walasek 2024.
agent_test: Not an agent test; calibration only: any agent lambda target must state the design (symmetric vs losses smaller than gains).

claim: The 2.25 median lambda of Tversky & Kahneman 1992 came from 25 graduate students, unincentivised, with only the median reported; it is not a population constant.
agent_test: Do not hard-code 2.25 as ground truth when scoring an agent; score against design-matched human meta-analytic values.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Loss aversion depends on the range of gains versus losses in the choice set: lambda 1.79 (gain range 40, loss range 20) vs 1.00-1.02 symmetric vs 0.88 reversed (Walasek & Stewart 2015, Exp 1a N=323); Exp 2 (N=401) gave 2.28; Exp 3 with real money (N=82) gave 1.81.
agent_test: Give the agent the same lotteries with offered gain/loss ranges swapped and check whether its choices shift as in humans; a robust agent should be stable on the same options.

claim: The 1979 core effects (certainty effect, reflection, isolation, small-probability overweighting) replicate: 94% of items and 12 of 13 contrasts in 19 countries (N=4,098), attenuated in size.
agent_test: Reuse original problems P1-P14 as an agent battery; compare agent choice shares to 1979 and 2020 shares.

claim: A newer territorial-prospect-theory replication replicates less well: item level 69% (US, N=149) and 81% (UK, N=253); contrasts 77% and 92%. Gap search: the OSF record is a PsyArXiv preprint (v2, Jul-Aug 2025); theoretical contrasts replicated 77% (US) and 92% (UK); reflection effect not robust; no journal peer review found.
agent_test: Caution only; verify preprint status before citing.

claim: Probability weighting and the fourfold pattern hold up better than loss aversion: human meta-analytic weighting about 0.68 and curvature about 0.67 (Imai 2025, read second-hand).
agent_test: Test whether the agent over-weights small and under-weights large stated probabilities at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs show modest loss aversion on average: pooled lambda 1.26 (95% CI 1.06-1.46; 28 estimates, 11 studies, 32 models), well below human 1.96, with prediction interval 0.20-2.31.
agent_test: Re-estimate lambda on our agent with a multiple-price list at baseline vs scaffold. All four lines are one author's preprint, so independence is 1.

claim: LLM loss aversion is human-like only in symmetric designs (1.15 vs 1.07) and much weaker where humans are strongest (1.46 vs 2.3).
agent_test: Run both symmetric and loss<gain designs on our agent and report both.

claim: LLM loss aversion varies enormously by model and version: 0.01 (Llama-3.1-8B) to 6.32 (Claude-3-Opus) to the 4.0 bound (GPT-5-mini); GPT-3.5 2.72 vs GPT-4.1 0.57. Family and release year explain part (Gemini +0.69, -0.16 per year).
schema_part: G (do not trust one model's behaviour profile)
agent_test: Measure our agent's lambda per backbone and per run; report SD (Jia found SD up to 2.84).

claim: LLM prospect-theory estimates are unstable: the same model's lambda moved 0.953 to 2.013 across rounds, verbal probability phrases were mapped differently by 7B vs 32B models, and models under 14B gave unreliable fits.
agent_test: Repeat lambda elicitation at least 5 times with different seeds and wordings; accept only if the CI is narrow.

claim: Describing loss aversion in the prompt changes LLM loss aversion: ChatGPT-4o lambda 1.09 with no paper, 1.79 after the abstract, 1.52 after the full report; Qwen same direction. Literature in prompt or training data may cause the measured bias. Tested only in ChatGPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B; no reasoning models; same lab as K07 so independence stays 1.
agent_test: Check whether the scaffold's own text names biases and thereby induces them; compare with and without bias vocabulary at equal tokens.

claim: Framing effects in LLMs are real but scenario dependent: ChatGPT rated 5 vs 4 in 11 of 11 trials (gain vs loss frame); in a 5-model study Championship shifted +1.40 to +1.84 while Career Transition reversed (-0.37 to -0.60); contradictory answers 57-85% in one drug scenario.
agent_test: Test the agent on matched gain/loss reframings of the same options; count flips with and without a re-frame step.

claim: LLM risk behaviour is shaped by persona: GPT-4.1 poor persona 37.39 rounds vs rich 1.11 (d=4.15, 6,950 decisions); Claude lambda fell 6.32 to 2.17 under real-world personas; personality traits correlate with lambda (r up to -0.68). Caveat from gap search: persona prompts also carried different goal text (Poor: 'take calculated risks'; Rich: 'avoid unnecessary risk'), so d=4.15 is persona plus goal; leakage to neutral tasks untested.
agent_test: Add persona or stake context to otherwise identical gambles and measure decision drift.

claim: Simple prompting rarely removes bias: direct and zero-shot CoT gave no reliable shift on loss aversion, one-shot examples shifted it, prompt detail cut most biases by up to 14.9%, models over 32B reduce bias in 39.5% of cases.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare direct, CoT, one-shot and a scaffold re-frame step on a bias battery with loss-aversion items.

claim: Prospect-theory machinery is used in LLM training: KTO takes alpha 0.88 and lambda 2.25 as template and beats DPO by 13.5 points on GSM8K (53.5 vs 40.0, Zephyr-beta-SFT) and with 90% of desirable examples dropped.
agent_test: Background only (training side). Do not claim loss aversion itself drives the gain.

claim: LLM-fitted PT parameters can improve simulation: route-choice agents with lambda 1.43 gave total error 0.0682 vs 0.6634 with non-travel parameters (.99/.99/2.25).
agent_test: Relevant only if the agent simulates humans; not a thinking-quality test.

claim: Anti-gambling mitigation claims (24.3% vs 52.4% fewer loss-chasing errors) are inconsistent between abstract and results and should not be used.
agent_test: Skip; do not use these numbers.

claim: LLM affect ratings are asymmetric (gain scale above loss scale in 8 of 9 post-trained models) while choice lambda stays near 1 (about 1.005-1.59), so feeling asymmetry does not translate into loss-averse choice.
agent_test: Compare the agent's stated ratings with its choices on the same items; flag mismatch.

claim: Reasoning models behave close to risk-neutral expected-payoff maximisers on lottery items and are order, framing and explanation invariant; conversational models do not. In 20 LLMs, RM-vs-EV choice correlation was 0.86 to 1, CM-vs-EV below 0.5, best LLM-human correlation only 0.42. Reasoning models are further from humans than chat models. Separately, extra thinking tokens did not reduce bias in vignette tests (Delta +0.031, p=.157).
agent_test: Run the same lottery and gain/loss framing items on the agent in thinking and non-thinking modes; compare to an EV-maximiser and to design-matched human shares. Do not assume EV-like is the right target when human values matter.

claim: Description versus history presentation (description-history gap) moves LLM choices toward humans and away from EV: small for frontier reasoning models (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-R1), large for conversational models and for open reasoning models of 7B to 32B. It is a bigger lever than gain/loss framing for chat models. Per-model decisiveness numbers are only in figures.
agent_test: Present the same decision once with stated odds and once as a list of past outcomes; log whether the agent's choice flips.

claim: Targeted debiasing steps lower bias scores in LLMs: SACD (detect, analyse, rewrite, up to 3 rounds) took average bias from 0.3805 to 0.1570 (FOMC, llama3.1-8b) and 0.4730 to 0.0560 (PubMedQA, 70b); DeFrame reduced fairness framing disparity 92% on BBQ at 4 calls per question. Task accuracy at equal tokens was not reported in either paper, 'loss aversion' in SACD is a punishment-warning prompt not lambda, and CoT, few-shot and debate sometimes raised bias.
agent_test: Add a re-frame-and-compare step; measure framing flips and task accuracy at equal total tokens against plain and against CoT.

claim: Describing human loss aversion in the prompt (or giving papers about it) raises LLM loss aversion in ChatGPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B; reasoning models untested.
agent_test: Compare agent lambda or flips with and without a bias-describing paragraph in the context, in a reasoning model too.

claim: Human loss-aversion moderators in the Brown et al. meta-analysis: field and general-population samples higher, surveys lower, money type no clear difference, only 14.4% of heterogeneity explained, funnel asymmetry strongest for means and aggregates. Mean 1.955 [1.824, 2.104], raw median 1.69, 607 estimates from 150 articles. No design-matched human lambda exists in the sources found; symmetric-unordered gives 1.07.
agent_test: State the design when comparing an agent's lambda: choose 1.07 for symmetric lotteries, 1.8 to 2.0 for loss-skewed ones.

claim: Prospect theory fits LLM choices poorly for some models and lambda estimates can sit at fit bounds: Llama-3.1-8B lambda 0.010 (R2 0.092), Qwen2.5-14B R2 0.067, GPT-5-Mini lambda 4.000; Qwen2.5-32B 1.213 (R2 0.225); human 2.63. Verbal probabilities shift lambda and weighting more than risk preference.
agent_test: Report fit quality, samples per lottery (256 used here) and wording spread with any agent lambda.

claim: KTO loss weights (lambda_D, lambda_U) are training hyperparameters only; no scaffold-side or inference-time use of loss weighting was found.
agent_test: None; background.
